summary.text: Lesson 2-5 of enVision Math Grade 4: subtracting with regrouping — what the trade really is, the addition check, and the flip error that dodges regroups by subtracting digits in the wrong direction.

why.text: Subtraction with regrouping is the first algorithm where a wrong method can feel perfectly smooth — the flip error never gets stuck, it just gets wrong answers. Learning to catch it with the addition check is the real lesson.

objectives.text: Check a subtraction by adding the difference to the subtrahend
Explain a regroup as a ten-for-one trade that keeps the value
Recognize and name the flip error

parentNote.text: Built from the Topic 2 textbook scan, Lesson 2-5. THE thing to watch in her written work: the flip error — subtracting the smaller digit from the larger regardless of which is on top. It never jams, so it feels fine while producing wrong answers. The habit that beats it is the addition check, which two questions here are built around. A difference is also framed as a gap on the number line — that picture pays off in 2-7.

nextUp.text: Cards, then the quiz in one sitting. Check one subtraction by adding — feel how fast it is.

cards.def:
**When a digit is too small to subtract from, trade 1 of the next place for 10 of this one.**
• 358 − 172: only 5 tens on top, 7 tens to remove — so 3 hundreds 5 tens becomes 2 hundreds 15 tens.
• It is the addition carry running in reverse.

**Difference + what you subtracted = what you started with.**
• 358 − 172 = 186, and the check is 186 + 172 = 358.
• Addition undoes subtraction — the check costs one easy addition and catches almost everything.
cards.hint: Add your answer to the number you took away. You should land exactly where you started.

cards.def:
**You cannot dodge a regroup by subtracting the digits in whichever order is easier.**
• In 534 − 278, the ones are 4 − 8. Flipping to 8 − 4 quietly changes the problem.
• The top number owns the digits. When its digit is small, regroup — never flip.
cards.hint: If you ever subtract upward in a column, stop. That column needed a trade.

cards.def:
**Subtraction measures the gap between two numbers on the number line.**
• Slide both numbers the same amount and the gap does not move: 600 − 250 and 650 − 300 are both 350.
• This picture is why counting up works, and why the across-zeros trick will work in 2-7.

questions.hint: The tens column needs a trade.
steps: Ones: 8 − 2 = 6. No trade needed.
Tens: 5 − 7 cannot go. Trade 1 hundred for 10 tens: now 15 − 7 = 8.
Hundreds: 2 − 1 = 1. Difference: 186.

ex.main: **186.** One trade in the tens; the flipped-digit answer 226 is the trap this lesson exists to close.
ex.tip: Check it: 186 + 172 = 358. Ten seconds, total certainty.

questions.hint: Both the ones and the tens need trades.
steps: Ones: 5 − 7 cannot go. Trade a ten: 15 − 7 = 8.
Tens: after lending, 1 − 6 cannot go. Trade a hundred: 11 − 6 = 5.
Hundreds: 3 − 2 = 1. Difference: 158.

ex.main: **158.** Two trades back to back — each column borrowed exactly once.
ex.tip: The wrong answer 242 comes from flipping every short column. If no column ever seems to need a trade, be suspicious.

questions.q: To subtract 358 − 172, the 5 tens on top are too few to give up 7 tens. What trade fixes it?
opts: Trade 1 hundred for 10 tens — 3 hundreds 5 tens becomes 2 hundreds 15 tens
Swap the 5 and the 7 so the bigger digit is on top
Subtract the tens column in the other direction
questions.hint: Help comes from the next place to the left.
steps: The tens column is short: 5 on top, 7 to remove.
One hundred is worth exactly 10 tens.
Trade one across: 2 hundreds remain, and the tens column now holds 15.
15 − 7 = 8, and the problem moves on.

ex.main: **Trade 1 hundred for 10 tens.** The total on top never changed — it is just dressed differently.
ex.tip: Regrouping never changes a number's value, only its outfit. 300 + 50 + 8 and 200 + 150 + 8 are the same 358.

questions.q: A theater has 743 seats and 458 are taken. How many seats are empty?
steps: Ones: 3 − 8 cannot go. Trade a ten: 13 − 8 = 5.
Tens: after lending, 3 − 5 cannot go. Trade a hundred: 13 − 5 = 8.
Hundreds: 6 − 4 = 2. Empty seats: 285.

ex.tip: Word problems change nothing about the arithmetic — find the two numbers and the direction, then work as usual.

questions.hint: Rebuild the starting number from its two pieces.
steps: Subtraction split 612 into two pieces: the 347 removed and the 265 left.
The check reassembles them: 265 + 347.
If that lands on 612 — and it does — the subtraction was right.

ex.main: **265 + 347 = 612.** Difference plus subtracted amount rebuilds the start.
ex.tip: The check is always difference + subtrahend = start. The other combinations rebuild nothing.

opts: He flipped short columns — doing 8 − 4 in the ones instead of regrouping to take 8 from 14
He regrouped one time too many
He subtracted the hundreds column first
questions.hint: Check his ones digit: where could a 4 have come from?
steps: The ones ask for 4 − 8, which needs a regroup: 14 − 8 = 6.
Leo's ones digit is 4 — that is 8 − 4, the flip.
His tens digit 4 is 7 − 3 flipped the same way.
Regrouped properly, 534 − 278 = 256. The check 256 + 278 = 534 confirms it.

ex.main: **The flip error — the true difference is 256.** Flipping feels harmless because every column "works", which is exactly what makes it dangerous.
ex.tip: His check would have caught it: 344 + 278 = 622, not 534. The check exists for precisely this quiet kind of error.

questions.q: A bake sale starts with 850 cookies and sells 365. How many are left?
steps: Ones: 0 − 5 cannot go. Trade a ten: 10 − 5 = 5.
Tens: after lending, 4 − 6 cannot go. Trade a hundred: 14 − 6 = 8.
Hundreds: 7 − 3 = 4. Left over: 485.

ex.main: **485.** Two trades, and the estimate stood close by the whole time.
ex.tip: A zero on top of the ones is the most common trade trigger there is — expect it, do not fear it.

questions.q: In 9▢4 − 372 = 582, what digit is hiding under ▢?
questions.hint: Work column by column and ask what each one needed.
steps: Ones: 4 − 2 = 2. Matches the 2 in 582 with no trade.
Tens: ▢ − 7 must give 8. No single digit does that directly, so a trade happened: ▢ + 10 − 7 = 8, meaning ▢ = 5.
Hundreds: 9 lent one away, so 8 − 3 = 5. Matches.
The hidden digit is 5: 954 − 372 = 582.

ex.main: **5.** The tens column only works if it borrowed — the puzzle is really asking you to spot the trade.
ex.tip: When a column's numbers seem impossible, a regroup is usually hiding in it. That is true in puzzles and in checking your own work.

questions.q: Why does adding the difference back to what you subtracted ALWAYS return the starting number?
opts: Subtraction splits the start into two pieces — the amount removed and the amount left — and addition reassembles them
It only works when no regrouping happened
Because both numbers get rounded the same way
It is a lucky pattern that might fail someday
questions.hint: Think of the starting number as something cut in two.
steps: 358 − 172 cuts 358 into two pieces: the 172 taken and the 186 left.
Nothing vanished — every unit is in one piece or the other.
Adding the pieces back together must rebuild the whole: 186 + 172 = 358.
That is why the check works every single time, regroups or not.

ex.main: **Subtraction cuts; addition reassembles.** The two pieces always sum to the whole because nothing ever left the table.
ex.tip: This is what "inverse operations" means beneath the vocabulary: one operation undoes the cut the other one made.

questions.q: True or false, and why: if BOTH numbers in a subtraction grow by 50, the difference grows too.
opts: False — both numbers slide up together, so the gap between them stays exactly the same
True — there is more being subtracted
questions.hint: Picture both numbers on a number line, sliding together.
steps: Grow both by 50: 650 − 300 = 350.
The gap did not move, because both ends of it moved together.
Contrast with addition, where growing both addends grows the sum by both amounts.

ex.main: **False — the difference holds still.** A difference is a gap, and a gap ignores where it sits on the line.
ex.tip: This same-slide idea becomes an actual technique in lesson 2-7. You are meeting it early, as a reason.
